device.name: Roborock Robot Vacuum (local protocol)
device.notes:
Roborock vacuums (S/QV/Qrevo/Saros series) can be driven locally over TCP, which removes the cloud from the command path. The catch: even Home Assistant's local mode fetches the device's IP and per-device "local key" through a one-time Roborock cloud login, and map data + routines are still cloud-fetched. So this is a "one-time cloud, then local control" story, not a fully cloud-free one.
TRANSPORT: TCP port 58867. 4-byte big-endian length prefix, then a message with header = version ("1.0", 3 bytes) + sequence (4B) + random (4B) + timestamp (4B) + protocol id (2B). Payload = AES-128-ECB-encrypted JSON with a CRC32 appended. Key derivation: MD5(encode_timestamp(ts) + local_key + SALT). Protocol ids distinguish local (0/1, 2/3, 4/5) from cloud (101/102); the cloud MQTT path uses the same binary message format.
NOTE: A01-protocol devices (Dyad wet/dry vacuums, Zeo washers) are cloud-only (MQTT) and are NOT covered by this local TCP path.

openness.notes: The local protocol is not published and is cloud-account-gated (the local key must be fetched via a Roborock login). python-roborock is the reference implementation; KonradIT/roborock-remote documents the header/auth.

issued_to_client: Per-device local key (fetched from the Roborock cloud after login)
credentials.notes: The local key gates the AES-128-ECB TCP session and is obtained from the cloud. Onboarding is app-mediated and not documented here.

factory_reset.description:
Two different procedures with two different scopes, and the second is a recovery step rather than a routine one — the vendor frames it as what to do when the robot is not functioning after a system reset.
One operational detail worth passing to a user: if the robot waits more than an hour for a connection after a WiFi reset, it disables WiFi altogether and the reset has to be done again before it can be reconnected.
factory_reset.effect: The WiFi reset clears the stored network and returns the robot to waiting for a connection; the vendor states that cleaning schedules, WiFi and other settings return to factory values after a system reset. Expect the local token to change, so any client holding one must re-extract it.

procedures.basis: Roborock's S7 and S7 Max Ultra user manuals. The manuals name the two buttons with icons that did not survive text extraction; they are the pair under the upper cover, beside the WiFi indicator.
procedures.indicator: The voice alert "Resetting WiFi", then the WiFi indicator flashing slowly.
procedures.name: Reset WiFi from the two top buttons

steps.action: Open the upper cover and find the WiFi indicator.
Press and hold the two buttons together until the robot says "Resetting WiFi".
Wait for the WiFi indicator to flash slowly; the robot is now waiting for a connection.
steps.expect: Slow flashing WiFi indicator. After an hour with no connection the robot disables WiFi and the reset must be repeated.

procedures.basis: Roborock's S7 user manual, under Restore Factory Settings — framed as the step for a robot that is not working after a system reset.
procedures.indicator: The voice prompt "Restoring the initial version".
procedures.name: Restore factory settings (recovery)

steps.action: Press and hold the power button and at the same time press the Reset button, until the robot says "Restoring the initial version".
steps.expect: The robot is restored to factory settings.

cloud.local_alternative: Partial — commands and polling run locally over TCP 58867 once the local key is fetched, but the local key/IP enumeration and map/routine data still require the Roborock cloud. There is no documented fully-offline path.

methods.description: Log into a Roborock account (an email code is sent), enumerate devices via the cloud API, and fetch each device's local key + IP. Then connect directly on TCP 58867 for local commands and polling.

steps.action: Onboard the vacuum onto Wi-Fi with the Roborock app.
Log into the Roborock cloud, enumerate devices, and fetch the local key + IP.
Connect to the device on TCP 58867 and issue local commands with the local key.

setup.notes: The vacuum is onboarded onto Wi-Fi via the Roborock app. Local control then requires a one-time cloud login to enumerate the device and fetch its IP + local key; commands and polling are local thereafter, but map data and routines are always cloud-fetched.

rejoin.notes: Wi-Fi re-provisioning is via the Roborock app; a reset may rotate the local key, requiring a fresh cloud fetch.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. Port 58867, AES-128-ECB, the cloud-login->local-key flow and the header layout are from the Home Assistant roborock integration and KonradIT/roborock-remote (which credits python-roborock).
